usage: 하다 conjugates to 해요, not 하요
noun 행복 + 을, a set blessing
행복하게 turns it into an adverb 'happily'
examples: plain 요-form 행복해요 stating your own state
우리 가족은 작은 집에서도 행복하게 살아요.
Our family lives happily even in a small house.
행복하게 as the adverb 'happily' modifying 살다
오랜만에 친구를 다시 만나서 정말 행복했어요.
I was really happy to meet my friend again after a long time.
-아서 gives the cause, 행복했어요 is past tense
nuance: 행복하다 is the deep, lasting 'happy' you feel about your life, family, or whole situation — closer to 'content/blessed' than a quick thrill. The Sino-Korean root is 幸福 (幸 good-fortune + 福 blessing), so it literally frames happiness as 'being blessed with good fortune', which is why it suits weddings, life reflections, and the standard blessing 행복하세요 ('be happy / may you be happy'). Contrast it with 기쁘다, which is a momentary gladness about one specific event (good news, a gift): you are 기쁘다 the instant you pass an exam, but 행복하다 about your life as a whole. As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 행복해 → 행복해요 (never 행복하요), and the noun-modifying form is 행복한 사람. Biggest English-speaker trap: don't reach for 행복하다 every time you'd say 'happy' in English ('I'm happy you came', 'happy to help') — for those small, event-bound moments Korean uses 기쁘다 or 좋다, and overusing 행복하다 sounds melodramatic.

Using 행복하다 for tiny moments like 'I'm happy you texted me' — that sounds overblown. For a specific small event Koreans say 기뻐요 or 좋아요; save 행복하다 for deep, whole-life happiness.

usage: I am sad / it is sad
add -아하다 to describe someone else's sadness
examples: 요-form 슬퍼요 describing a thing that evokes sadness
When I listen to sad songs, tears come.
Everyone grieved because Grandmother passed away.
슬퍼하다 (not 슬퍼요) for a third person's visible grief
nuance: 슬프다 is the core 'sad' for sorrow, loss, and touching/heartbreaking things — both 'I feel sad' and 'this is sad' (a sad movie, sad news). It is an adjective rooted in your own felt emotion, so for your own heart you say 슬퍼요, but to report that someone ELSE is sad Korean grammar prefers the derived verb 슬퍼하다 ('to act sad/grieve'): 동생이 슬퍼해요, not 동생이 슬퍼요 — this 형용사 → -아하다 → 동사 shift is a real adjective rule, the same as 좋다 → 좋아하다. Spelling-wise it is a ㅡ(으) irregular: drop the ㅡ before an ending starting with 어, so 슬프 + 어요 → 슬퍼요, and the modifier is 슬픈. Don't confuse 슬프다 with 우울하다 (憂鬱, 'depressed/gloomy'), which is a heavier, longer-lasting low mood rather than acute sorrow. Pitfall: writing 슬프어요 — the ㅡ must drop, giving 슬퍼요.

usage: the textbook collocation for happy news
note: greetings use 반갑다, not 기쁘다
examples: I'm glad because I heard good news.
-아서 cause + 기뻐요, tied to a specific event
I was really glad that I passed the exam.
past tense 기뻤어요 about one happy event
My parents were glad too at the news of my passing.
기뻐하다 + honorific -시 for parents' visible joy
nuance: 기쁘다 is gladness aimed at a SPECIFIC good event — good news, a success, a gift, a reunion — the spark of joy in the moment, not a settled state of life. This is exactly the line versus 행복하다: you are 기쁘다 the second you pass an exam, but 행복하다 about your life overall; reaching for 행복하다 for small wins sounds theatrical, while 기쁘다 fits them perfectly. Like 슬프다 it is a ㅡ irregular, so 기쁘 + 어요 → 기뻐요 (never 기쁘어요), modifier 기쁜. For another person's joy, shift to the verb 기뻐하다 (동생이 기뻐해요). A key English-speaker trap: 'glad/nice to meet you' is NOT 만나서 기뻐요 — Korean fixes that greeting as 만나서 반가워요 (from 반갑다), so save 기쁘다 for being glad about news and outcomes, not for the social 'nice to meet you.'

Using 기쁘다 for deep life happiness ('I'm happy with my life' → 기뻐요?). That should be 행복해요; 기쁘다 is event-bound momentary gladness.

usage: the full underlying phrase 화 + 가 + 나다
화 + 를 + 내다 = actively vent anger
examples: I get angry when I hear those words.
I got angry because my friend broke our promise.
화를 내다 + honorific 내셨어요 for actively showing anger
nuance: 화나다 is anger that RISES in you in the moment — it is literally 화가 나다, where 화 (火, 'fire/wrath') is the anger and 나다 means 'to arise/come out', so the image is 'the fire comes up.' Because the verb is 나다, the form is 화나요 / 화났어요 — there is no 하다 here, so 화나해요 is wrong. Crucially, distinguish 화나다 from 화내다 (화를 내다): 화나다 is the inner feeling that arises ('I become/am angry'), while 화내다 is OUTWARDLY venting it at someone ('to get mad at / yell at'). So 나한테 화났어 = 'you're angry at me (you feel it)', but 나한테 화내지 마 = 'don't take your anger out on me.' Note also that the person you're angry at is marked with 한테/에게 (사람한테 화나다), which English 'angry at' doesn't visibly mark. For describing a face or person, the modifier is the past form 화난 (화난 표정). A blunter near-synonym is 짜증나다 ('to be irritated/annoyed'), a lighter, more peevish irritation than full 화.

examples: 요-form 피곤해요 for your own bodily state
I'm so tired because I worked overtime.
I'm tired, and on top of that trying to exercise is hard.
-ㄴ데 'tired, and' giving background before the main point
nuance: 피곤하다 is physical/general tiredness — worn out, drained, exhausted — typically after work, study, travel, or poor sleep. It is Sino-Korean 疲困 (疲 weary + 困 exhausted), literally 'weary-exhausted', which is why it reads as bodily fatigue rather than sleepiness. Keep it apart from 졸리다 ('sleepy'): you can be 피곤하다 yet wide awake (drained but not nodding off), and 졸리다 is specifically wanting to sleep — don't swap them. It is also milder and more everyday than 지치다 ('to be worn out/burned out'), which implies you've reached your limit. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 피곤해요 (not 피곤하요). One common English-speaker slip: 피곤하다 normally describes a PERSON being tired; to call an activity 'tiring' you also use 피곤하다 (피곤한 일 = 'tiring work'), but to call a person 'tiresome/draining' Koreans say 피곤한 사람 — meaning 'a person who is exhausting to deal with', a nuance worth knowing so you don't misread it as 'a tired person.'

Using 피곤하다 to mean 'sleepy.' Drained-but-awake is 피곤하다; wanting to sleep is 졸리다. 'I'm sleepy' = 졸려요, not 피곤해요.

usage: noun 졸음 + 이 + 오다, a set phrase
-아서 죽겠다 = casual hyperbole 'so sleepy I could die'
examples: 요-form 졸려요 for your own drowsy state
After eating lunch, I got sleepy.
The class is boring, so I keep getting sleepy.
nuance: 졸리다 is the specific feeling of drowsiness — your eyelids drooping, wanting to fall asleep — and it is the everyday way to say 'I'm sleepy.' Sharply separate it from 피곤하다 ('tired'): 피곤하다 is being physically drained (you can be exhausted yet alert), while 졸리다 is purely the urge to sleep, so after a heavy lunch you're 졸리다, but after a marathon you're 피곤하다. Conjugation: the stem 졸리 + 어요 contracts the ㅣ+ㅓ into 려, giving 졸려요 (never 졸리어요), and the modifier is 졸린 (졸린 눈). A closely related word is the noun 졸음 ('drowsiness'), used in 졸음이 오다 ('drowsiness comes') and 졸음운전 ('drowsy driving'). English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'I'm sleepy' as 졸려워요 by wrongly treating it like a ㅂ-irregular — 졸리다 is a plain ㅣ-stem, so it is 졸려요. Also resist saying 잠이 와요 thinking it's wrong; that's actually a perfectly natural synonym ('sleep is coming'), interchangeable with 졸려요.

usage: the literal underlying form 배 + 가 + 고프다
-아 죽겠다 casual hyperbole 'so hungry I could die'
examples: 요-form 배고파요 for your own state
I'm hungry because I skipped breakfast.
I'm hungry, but all the restaurants are closed.
nuance: 배고프다 is the normal, everyday 'hungry' and is transparently a compound: 배 ('belly/stomach') + 고프다 ('to be empty/craving'), literally 'the stomach is empty' — which is why you'll also hear the spelled-out 배가 고프다 with the same meaning. The single bound word 고프다 is essentially only used with 배, so learn 배고프다 as a unit. Conjugation is the ㅡ irregular: drop the ㅡ before -아요, so 배고프 + 아요 → 배고파요 (note it takes 아, not 어, because the remaining vowel ㅗ is bright/positive); the modifier is 배고픈. Its natural opposite is 배부르다 ('to be full', a 르 irregular → 배불러요). English-speaker pitfalls: (1) writing 배고프아요 — the ㅡ must drop, giving 배고파요; (2) saying 나는 배고파요 in formal/polite company where 저는 is expected — 나는 is casual; (3) don't say 배고프다 to mean 'I want to eat that specific food' — that craving is 먹고 싶다, while 배고프다 is just the empty-stomach sensation.

usage: the literal underlying form 목 + 이 + 마르다
-아 죽겠다 casual hyperbole for intense thirst
examples: Please give me some water, I'm thirsty.
요-form 목말라요 plus a polite request
I'm thirsty because the weather is hot.
nuance: 목마르다 means 'thirsty' and is literally 목 ('throat/neck') + 마르다 ('to dry up'), i.e. 'the throat goes dry' — you'll equally hear the unpacked 목이 마르다. The base verb 마르다 also means 'to dry' in general (빨래가 마르다 = 'the laundry dries') and even 'to be skinny' (몸이 말랐다), so context tells you which. The conjugation is the classic 르 irregular: before -아/어 the 르 doubles its ㄹ and the preceding syllable takes the added ㄹ, so 마르 + 아요 → 말라요, giving 목말라요 (modifier 목마른). Compare 모르다 → 몰라요 and 빠르다 → 빨라요 — same mechanism. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) the #1 error is writing 목마르아요 as if it were regular — it must be 목말라요; (2) don't confuse it with 배고프다; thirst is 목마르다, hunger is 배고프다, and they are not interchangeable; (3) figuratively 목마르다 can mean 'to thirst/crave' (성공에 목마르다 = 'thirsty for success'), a nuance English shares, so that idiom does transfer.

Treating 마르다 as only 'thirsty.' It also means 'to dry' (빨래가 마르다) and 'to be thin' (말랐다). For thirst you specifically need 목(이) 마르다.

usage: as a way to kill boredom
examples: I'm bored because I have nothing to do.
주말에 심심하면 우리 집에 놀러 와.
If you're bored on the weekend, come hang out at my place.
I'm so bored being home alone.
nuance: 심심하다 is the boredom you feel as a PERSON when you have nothing to do — restless, twiddling your thumbs, 'I'm bored.' This is the crucial contrast with 지루하다: 심심하다 describes the bored SUBJECT (a person with empty time → 나는 심심해), whereas 지루하다 describes a boring OBJECT/experience that drags (a dull movie or lecture → 영화가 지루해). So 'I'm bored' (nothing to do) is 심심해요, but 'this class is boring' is 이 수업이 지루해요 — swapping them is the classic learner error. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 심심해요 (not 심심하요). It pairs naturally with 심심하면 ~ ('if you're bored, ...') as a soft invitation, and with the fixed nouns 심심풀이 ('a pastime/something to kill time'). usage: the feared thing takes 이/가, not 을/를
-아하다 verb for a third person's fear
examples: 요-form 무서워요 describing a frightening thing
높은 곳이 — the feared thing marked with 이/가
My little sibling is afraid of dark rooms.
무서워하다 + 을/를 for another person's fear
nuance: 무섭다 covers both 'scary' (a thing is frightening: 무서운 영화) and 'afraid' (you feel fear: 개가 무서워요), and it carries a key grammar quirk shared by emotion adjectives like 좋다/싫다: the THING you fear is marked with 이/가, not the object 을/를 — so 'I'm afraid of dogs' is 개가 무서워요 (literally 'dogs are scary-to-me'), which trips up English speakers who expect 'fear' to take a direct object. When you switch to describing someone ELSE's fear, you must use the derived verb 무서워하다, and THEN the feared thing takes 을/를: 동생이 개를 무서워해요. Conjugation is the ㅂ irregular — ㅂ turns into 우 before a vowel — so 무섭 + 어요 → 무서워요 and the modifier is 무서운 (not 무섭은). Distinguish it from 무섭다's relatives: 두렵다 is a more literary, abstract dread (미래가 두렵다 = 'I dread the future'), while 무섭다 is the everyday, gut-level scary; and 겁나다 is a casual 'I'm freaked out.' Pitfall: never write 무섭어요 — the ㅂ must become 우.

examples: It's more fun because I'm with friends.
I had a good time during the vacation.
nuance: 즐겁다 is 'enjoyable/fun' centered on an ACTIVITY or shared time — a trip, a party, a class, time with friends — the pleasant feeling of doing something. It is the standard word in well-wishes like 즐거운 하루 보내세요 ('have a nice day') and 즐거운 여행 ('a pleasant trip'). Contrast it with 재미있다, its close cousin: 재미있다 leans toward 'interesting/amusing/funny' (a gripping book or a funny video can be 재미있다 even alone), while 즐겁다 emphasizes your overall enjoyment of a situation or time spent — a quiet family dinner is 즐겁다 more than 재미있다. Conjugation is the ㅂ irregular: ㅂ → 우 before a vowel, so 즐겁 + 어요 → 즐거워요, and the modifier is 즐거운 (not 즐겁은). The adverb 즐겁게 ('enjoyably') is extremely common with verbs like 놀다/지내다. English-speaker pitfall: don't default to 재미있다 for every 'fun' — for 'have a good time' and pleasant shared occasions, Koreans reach for 즐겁다; and never write 즐겁어요 (the ㅂ must become 우).

Forming the modifier as 즐겁은 여행. The ㅂ-irregular noun-modifier is 즐거운 → 즐거운 여행.

usage: the boring thing takes 이/가 as subject
I'm bored to death (it's so dull)
examples: This book is a bit boring.
요-form 지루해요 describing a tedious thing
The meeting was so long that it got boring.
If the movie is boring, you can just sleep.
nuance: 지루하다 is 'boring/tedious' for something that DRAGS — a long meeting, a dull movie, a slow lecture — the quality of an experience that wears your patience thin. This is the mirror image of 심심하다, and keeping them straight is one of the most useful distinctions in this set: 지루하다 describes the boring THING/experience (영화가 지루해 = 'the movie is boring'), while 심심하다 describes a bored PERSON with nothing to do (나는 심심해 = 'I'm bored'). So 'I'm bored' (idle) ≠ 'this is boring' (tedious) — the first is 심심해요, the second 지루해요. As a regular 하다-adjective it is 지루해요 (not 지루하요), modifier 지루한. A near-synonym is 따분하다, which is similar 'dull/tedious' with a slightly more listless, fed-up flavor; 지루하다 is the neutral default. English-speaker pitfall: because English uses one word 'boring/bored' for both the cause and the feeler, learners say 나는 지루해요 meaning 'I'm bored' — but that literally implies 'I am a boring thing.' For your own idle boredom say 심심해요; reserve 지루하다 for the tedious thing itself.
